ramayana-3-1-1.translation: Entering the vast Dandaka forest, the self-possessed and unconquerable Rama saw a circle of hermitages of ascetics.
ramayana-3-1-1.meaning: The exile enters its next stage: the deep forest, where holy people live.
ramayana-3-1-1.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-2.translation: It was strewn with kusha grass and bark garments and filled with spiritual radiance, as hard to look at as the blazing disc of the sun in the sky.
ramayana-3-1-2.meaning: The hermitage glowed with the power of holy living.
ramayana-3-1-2.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-3.translation: It was a refuge for all creatures, its courtyards always swept clean, honoured and danced in by troupes of apsaras.
ramayana-3-1-3.meaning: It was a safe place for every living being, kept clean and holy.
ramayana-3-1-3.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-4.translation: It was adorned with large fire-sanctuaries, ladles and vessels, deerskins, kusha grass, firewood, water pots, fruits and roots.
ramayana-3-1-4.meaning: The place was full of the simple tools of daily worship.
ramayana-3-1-4.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-5.translation: It was surrounded by great sacred forest trees bearing sweet fruit, worshipped with offerings and oblations, and resounding with Vedic chanting.
ramayana-3-1-5.meaning: Nature and prayer filled the hermitage together.
ramayana-3-1-5.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-6.translation: It was strewn with wild flowers and had a lotus pond; and the sages there lived on fruits and roots, were self-controlled, and wore bark and black deerskin.
ramayana-3-1-6.meaning: The sages lived simply and with self-discipline.
ramayana-3-1-6.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-7.translation: It was surrounded by ancient sages bright as the sun and fire, and adorned with great seers of holy, restrained diet.
ramayana-3-1-7.meaning: Old and holy sages, shining with their practice, lived there.
ramayana-3-1-7.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-8.translation: Resounding with Vedic chanting, like the abode of Brahma itself, it was graced by noble brahmins who knew the Absolute.
ramayana-3-1-8.meaning: The hermitage felt like heaven on earth.
ramayana-3-1-8.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-9.translation: Seeing that circle of hermitages, the glorious and mighty Rama unstrung his great bow and approached.
ramayana-3-1-9.meaning: Rama lowered his weapon out of respect before entering a holy place.
ramayana-3-1-9.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them. Unstringing the bow is a sign of peaceful intent.

ramayana-3-1-10.translation: The great seers, endowed with divine insight, saw Rama and the renowned Sita and came forward joyfully to meet them.
ramayana-3-1-10.meaning: The sages were glad to see Rama and Sita.
ramayana-3-1-10.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-11.translation: Seeing him like the rising moon, those righteous sages firm in their vows received him, speaking words of blessing.
ramayana-3-1-11.meaning: The sages blessed Rama as he arrived.
ramayana-3-1-11.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-12.translation: Amazed, they gazed at the form, build, grace, gentleness and fine dress of Rama the forest-dweller.
ramayana-3-1-12.meaning: Even in exile Rama's nobility shone through.
ramayana-3-1-12.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-13.translation: All the forest-dwellers gazed at Sita, Lakshmana and Rama with unblinking eyes, as at a wonder.
ramayana-3-1-13.meaning: The three were a marvel to the sages.
ramayana-3-1-13.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-14.translation: Those noble sages, devoted to the welfare of all beings, lodged Rama as their guest in a leaf hut.
ramayana-3-1-14.meaning: The sages welcomed Rama as an honoured guest.
ramayana-3-1-14.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-15.translation: Then the noble, righteous sages, bright as fire, honoured Rama by due rite and brought him water.
ramayana-3-1-15.meaning: They offered him the traditional welcome.
ramayana-3-1-15.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-16.translation: Offering him roots, flowers, forest fruits and the hermitage itself, those who knew dharma spoke with joined palms.
ramayana-3-1-16.meaning: The sages gave all they had, then made a humble request.
ramayana-3-1-16.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-17.translation: The king is the protector of dharma for his people, their famous refuge, worthy of worship and honour, the bearer of the rod of justice, and their elder.
ramayana-3-1-17.meaning: A true ruler protects what is right and shelters his people.
ramayana-3-1-17.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

keywords.meaning: bearer of the rod of justice

ramayana-3-1-18.translation: O Rama, the king protects his subjects as a fourth part of Indra; therefore the king, honoured by the world, enjoys fine things.
ramayana-3-1-18.meaning: A ruler's privileges come with the duty to protect.
ramayana-3-1-18.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-19.translation: We who live in your realm must be protected by you; whether you live in the city or in the forest, you are our king, lord of the people.
ramayana-3-1-19.meaning: Rama is still their king, even in exile.
ramayana-3-1-19.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-20.translation: O king, we have laid down the rod of force, conquered anger and mastered our senses; we ascetics must always be protected by you, like a child in the womb.
ramayana-3-1-20.meaning: Those who have given up violence rely on the just to protect them.
ramayana-3-1-20.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-21.translation: Having said this, they honoured Rama and Lakshmana with fruits, roots, wild flowers and many other foods.
ramayana-3-1-21.meaning: The sages showed their love with simple gifts.
ramayana-3-1-21.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-1-22.translation: Likewise other ascetics, perfected and bright as fire, upright in conduct, properly gratified the lord Rama.
ramayana-3-1-22.meaning: All the sages welcomed Rama fittingly.
ramayana-3-1-22.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 1: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana enter the Dandaka forest and are welcomed by the sages living there, who ask Rama to protect them.

ramayana-3-2-1.translation: Having received hospitality, Rama took leave of all the sages at sunrise and plunged deeper into the forest.
ramayana-3-2-1.meaning: Rama moved on into the wild, dangerous forest.
ramayana-3-2-1.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-2.translation: It was crowded with many kinds of deer, haunted by tigers and wolves, its trees, creepers and shrubs broken, its pools hard to see.
ramayana-3-2-2.meaning: The forest became dark and threatening.
ramayana-3-2-2.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-3.translation: Followed by Lakshmana, Rama saw the heart of the forest, loud with crickets and many kinds of birds.
ramayana-3-2-3.meaning: They went into the deep forest.
ramayana-3-2-3.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-4.translation: There, in the middle of that forest full of fierce beasts, Rama saw a man-eater as large as a mountain peak, with a mighty roar.
ramayana-3-2-4.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-5.translation: He had deep-set eyes, a huge mouth, a monstrous shape and a misshapen belly; he was loathsome, crooked, tall, deformed and frightful to see.
ramayana-3-2-5.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-6.translation: He wore a tiger skin wet with fat and splashed with blood, terrifying to all beings, his mouth gaping like Death.
ramayana-3-2-6.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-7.translation: He had three lions, four tigers, two wolves, ten spotted deer and a great elephant's head with its tusks, smeared with fat,
ramayana-3-2-7.meaning: He carried his kills with him.
ramayana-3-2-7.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-8.translation: impaled on an iron spear, roaring loudly. Seeing Rama, Lakshmana and Sita of Mithila,
ramayana-3-2-8.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-9.translation: he rushed at them in fury like Death at living creatures, and let out a terrible roar as if shaking the earth.
ramayana-3-2-9.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-10.translation: Snatching up Sita, he moved off and said: 'You two wear matted hair and bark, yet have a wife with you; your lives are nearly over,
ramayana-3-2-10.meaning: He seized Sita and mocked the brothers.
ramayana-3-2-10.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-11.translation: you have entered the Dandaka forest carrying arrows, bows and swords. How is it that two ascetics live with a woman?
ramayana-3-2-11.meaning: He accused them of being false ascetics.
ramayana-3-2-11.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-12.translation: Who are you, wicked ones doing wrong and disgracing the sages? I am the demon named Viradha, roaming this impassable forest,
ramayana-3-2-12.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-13.translation: always armed and eating the flesh of seers. This lovely woman will be my wife, and I will drink the blood of you two sinners in battle.'
ramayana-3-2-13.meaning: He threatened them with death and claimed Sita.
ramayana-3-2-13.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-14.translation: Hearing the bold and arrogant words of the wicked Viradha, Sita, daughter of Janaka, was alarmed and trembled with fear like a plantain tree in a gale.
ramayana-3-2-14.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-15.translation: Seeing the lovely Sita in Viradha's grip, Rama spoke to Lakshmana with his mouth gone dry:
ramayana-3-2-15.meaning: Rama was shaken with fear for Sita.
ramayana-3-2-15.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-16.translation: 'Look, gentle one, at the daughter of King Janaka, my virtuous wife, raised in great comfort, a famous princess, now in Viradha's grip.
ramayana-3-2-16.meaning: Rama grieved to see Sita in danger.
ramayana-3-2-16.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-17.translation: What Kaikeyi wanted for us, the boon she chose, has quickly come true this very day, Lakshmana.
ramayana-3-2-17.meaning: In his anguish Rama recalls the exile that brought them here.
ramayana-3-2-17.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon. Rama's bitterness here is a moment of human grief, not his settled view.

ramayana-3-2-18.translation: She who, far-sighted for her son, was not satisfied with the kingdom, and by whom I, a friend of all beings, was sent to the forest, my middle mother has now got her wish.
ramayana-3-2-18.meaning: Rama voices pain at Kaikeyi's wish.
ramayana-3-2-18.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-19.translation: Nothing gives me greater pain, Lakshmana, than another's touch on Sita, not even my father's death or the loss of my kingdom.
ramayana-3-2-19.meaning: Rama feels Sita's danger more deeply than any loss of his own.
ramayana-3-2-19.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-20.translation: As Rama spoke, flooded with tears and grief, Lakshmana, angry, said, hissing like a trapped serpent:
ramayana-3-2-20.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-21.translation: 'You are the protector of all beings, like Indra; why do you grieve like one without protection, when I am your servant?
ramayana-3-2-21.meaning: Lakshmana reminds Rama of his strength.
ramayana-3-2-21.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-22.translation: Today the earth will drink the blood of the demon Viradha, slain by my arrow in anger.
ramayana-3-2-22.meaning: Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.
ramayana-3-2-22.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-23.translation: The anger I felt toward Bharata, who wanted the kingdom, I will release on Viradha, as Indra hurls his thunderbolt at a mountain.
ramayana-3-2-23.meaning: Lakshmana turns his old anger toward a rightful target.
ramayana-3-2-23.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-2-24.translation: Driven by the force of my arms, let my great arrow fall on his broad chest, take away his life, and let him fall reeling to the ground.'
ramayana-3-2-24.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 2: the demon Viradha attacks, seizes Sita, and Rama is overcome with grief while Lakshmana vows to kill the demon.

ramayana-3-3-1.translation: Then Viradha spoke again, filling the forest with his voice: 'I am asking you: tell me, who are you and where will you go?'
ramayana-3-3-1.meaning: The demon demanded to know who they were.
ramayana-3-3-1.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-2.translation: The mighty Rama answered the demon with the blazing face, who was asking about his family line, the Ikshvakus:
ramayana-3-3-2.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-3.translation: 'Know us to be two kshatriyas of good conduct, wandering the forest. But we want to know you: who are you, roaming the Dandaka?'
ramayana-3-3-3.meaning: Rama gave a calm, honest answer.
ramayana-3-3-3.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-4.translation: Viradha said to Rama, whose valour was true: 'Listen, king, I will tell you; learn about me, Rama.
ramayana-3-3-4.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-5.translation: I am the son of Java, and my mother is Shatahrada; all the demons on earth call me Viradha.
ramayana-3-3-5.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-6.translation: By my austerity I have gained, by Brahma's grace, the power not to be killed by weapons, and to be uncut and unpierced.
ramayana-3-3-6.meaning: He boasted of a boon that made him hard to kill.
ramayana-3-3-6.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-7.translation: Leave this woman, go back the way you came and save yourselves quickly; I will not take your lives.'
ramayana-3-3-7.meaning: He offered to spare them if they gave up Sita.
ramayana-3-3-7.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-8.translation: Rama, his eyes red with anger, answered the misshapen, evil-minded demon Viradha:
ramayana-3-3-8.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-9.translation: 'Shame on you, low one, with your vile purpose; you are surely seeking death. Stand and fight; you will not leave me alive.'
ramayana-3-3-9.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-10.translation: Then Rama strung his bow, quickly fitted very sharp arrows and struck the demon.
ramayana-3-3-10.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-11.translation: From his bow with its taut string he released seven arrows with golden feathers, very swift, as fast as Garuda or the wind.
ramayana-3-3-11.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-12.translation: Piercing the body of Viradha, who wore peacock feathers, the fiery arrows fell to the ground smeared with blood.
ramayana-3-3-12.meaning: The arrows passed right through the demon.
ramayana-3-3-12.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-13.translation: Roaring loudly, he seized his spear, like Indra's banner, and looked like Death with open jaws.
ramayana-3-3-13.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-14.translation: That spear, like a thunderbolt and blazing like fire in the sky, Rama, best of warriors, cut apart with two arrows.
ramayana-3-3-14.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-15.translation: Lakshmana broke the fierce demon's left arm, and Rama forcefully broke his right arm.
ramayana-3-3-15.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-16.translation: With his arms broken, the alarmed demon fell quickly to the ground like a cloud, like a mountain split by a thunderbolt, and said to Rama, the best of men:
ramayana-3-3-16.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-17.translation: 'Dear one, I recognise you as Rama, Kausalya's noble son; and the blessed Sita, and the renowned Lakshmana.
ramayana-3-3-17.meaning: In defeat Viradha recognised who Rama was.
ramayana-3-3-17.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-18.translation: Through a curse I entered this terrible demon body. I am the gandharva Tumburu, cursed by Kubera.
ramayana-3-3-18.meaning: He revealed he was a celestial being under a curse.
ramayana-3-3-18.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-19.translation: When I begged him for mercy, the famous one told me: "When Rama, son of Dasharatha, kills you in battle,
ramayana-3-3-19.meaning: He recalled how the curse could end.
ramayana-3-3-19.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-20.translation: then you will regain your true nature and go to heaven." So said King Kubera to me, who was attached to Rambha,
ramayana-3-3-20.meaning: Death at Rama's hand would free him.
ramayana-3-3-20.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-21.translation: angry because I had not attended on him. By your grace I am freed from that terrible curse. I will go to my own home; may all be well with you, scorcher of foes.
ramayana-3-3-21.meaning: Viradha was released and thanked Rama.
ramayana-3-3-21.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga. Being killed by Rama becomes liberation, a recurring theme in the epic.

ramayana-3-3-22.translation: Not far from here, a yojana and a half away, lives the righteous and powerful sage Sharabhanga, radiant like the sun.
ramayana-3-3-22.meaning: He pointed them to a holy sage.
ramayana-3-3-22.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

keywords.meaning: a measure of distance, several miles

ramayana-3-3-23.translation: Go to him quickly; he will do you good. And, Rama, put me in a pit and go on safely.
ramayana-3-3-23.meaning: He asked for burial and gave guidance.
ramayana-3-3-23.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-24.translation: This is the ancient custom for demons whose life has gone: those who are placed in a pit gain everlasting worlds.'
ramayana-3-3-24.meaning: He explained the custom for his kind.
ramayana-3-3-24.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-25.translation: Having said this to Rama, the mighty Viradha, wounded by arrows, left his body and reached heaven.
ramayana-3-3-25.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-26.translation: Lifting him up, still loudly roaring, with ears like spikes, they threw Viradha into the pit.
ramayana-3-3-26.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-3-27.translation: Having slain the demon and recovered Sita, the two with their gold-adorned bows roamed joyfully in the great forest, like the moon and sun in the sky.
ramayana-3-3-27.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 3: Rama and Lakshmana defeat Viradha, who turns out to be a cursed celestial musician released by his death, and he directs them to the sage Sharabhanga.

ramayana-3-4-1.translation: Having killed the demon Viradha of terrible strength, the valiant Rama embraced and comforted Sita, then spoke to his radiant brother Lakshmana:
ramayana-3-4-1.meaning: Rama comforted Sita after the danger.
ramayana-3-4-1.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-2.translation: 'This forest is hard and dangerous, and we are not used to forest life; let us go quickly to Sharabhanga, rich in austerity.'
ramayana-3-4-2.meaning: Rama sought guidance from a wise sage.
ramayana-3-4-2.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-3.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-4.translation: Near Sharabhanga, who had godlike power and a soul purified by austerity, he saw a great wonder.
ramayana-3-4-4.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-5.translation: He saw the lord of the gods, shining in body like the sun and fire, not touching the earth.
ramayana-3-4-5.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-6.translation: The god wore bright ornaments and spotless clothes, and was worshipped by many great souls like himself.
ramayana-3-4-6.meaning: Indra was surrounded by divine beings.
ramayana-3-4-6.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-7.translation: Not far away Rama saw his chariot standing in the sky, yoked to green horses, shining like the young sun.
ramayana-3-4-7.meaning: Indra's chariot hovered in the air.
ramayana-3-4-7.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-8.translation: He saw a spotless parasol, like a mass of white cloud or the moon's disc, adorned with bright garlands.
ramayana-3-4-8.meaning: A royal parasol marked Indra's rank.
ramayana-3-4-8.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-9.translation: Two excellent whisks with golden handles, very precious, were held by two women and waved over his head.
ramayana-3-4-9.meaning: Attendants fanned the king of gods.
ramayana-3-4-9.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-10.translation: Many gandharvas, gods, perfected beings and great seers praised the god in the sky with fine words.
ramayana-3-4-10.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-11.translation: Seeing Indra there, Rama said to Lakshmana: 'The heavenly horses of Indra we heard of long ago, travelling through the sky, these must be they.
ramayana-3-4-11.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-12.translation: And these young men standing around the chariot, tiger among men, a hundred and a hundred, wearing earrings and holding swords,
ramayana-3-4-12.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-13.translation: all with necklaces bright as fire on their chests, look twenty-five years old, Lakshmana.
ramayana-3-4-13.meaning: The divine guards looked young and radiant.
ramayana-3-4-13.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-14.translation: For that, they say, is the age the gods always have, just as these handsome tigers among men appear.
ramayana-3-4-14.meaning: The gods are said never to age.
ramayana-3-4-14.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-15.translation: Stay here with Sita for a moment, Lakshmana, until I find out clearly who this shining one in the chariot is.'
ramayana-3-4-15.meaning: Rama went ahead alone to see.
ramayana-3-4-15.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-16.translation: Having told Lakshmana 'Wait here', Rama walked toward Sharabhanga's hermitage.
ramayana-3-4-16.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-17.translation: Then Indra, husband of Shachi, seeing Rama approach, took leave of Sharabhanga and said to the gods:
ramayana-3-4-17.meaning: Indra prepared to leave as Rama came.
ramayana-3-4-17.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: approaching Sharabhanga's hermitage, Rama sees Indra, king of the gods, in his heavenly chariot.

ramayana-3-4-18.translation: 'Rama is coming here. Until he speaks to me, take me to my destination; only afterwards may he see me.
ramayana-3-4-18.meaning: Indra wished to leave before meeting Rama.
ramayana-3-4-18.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-19.translation: I will soon see him victorious and his purpose fulfilled; for he has a great deed to do that others could hardly do.'
ramayana-3-4-19.meaning: Indra foresees Rama's coming task, the defeat of Ravana.
ramayana-3-4-19.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-20.translation: So saying, the wielder of the thunderbolt took leave of the ascetic, honoured him, and went to heaven in his chariot drawn by green horses.
ramayana-3-4-20.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-21.translation: When the thousand-eyed god had gone, Rama with his companions approached Sharabhanga, who was attending to his fire offering.
ramayana-3-4-21.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-22.translation: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana touched his feet; given permission, invited and offered lodging, they sat down.
ramayana-3-4-22.meaning: They paid respect and were welcomed.
ramayana-3-4-22.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-23.translation: Then Rama asked about Indra's visit, and Sharabhanga told him everything.
ramayana-3-4-23.meaning: The sage explained why Indra had come.
ramayana-3-4-23.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-24.translation: 'Rama, this giver of boons wants to take me to Brahma's world, which I have won by fierce austerity and which is hard for the undisciplined to reach.
ramayana-3-4-24.meaning: The sage had earned the highest heaven.
ramayana-3-4-24.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-25.translation: But knowing you were near, tiger among men, I will not go to Brahma's world without seeing you, my dear guest.
ramayana-3-4-25.meaning: He waited to see Rama first.
ramayana-3-4-25.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-26.translation: Having met you, I will go to the heaven the gods dwell in. I have won imperishable, auspicious worlds, those of Brahma and of highest heaven; accept them from me.'
ramayana-3-4-26.meaning: The sage offered Rama all the merit he had earned.
ramayana-3-4-26.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-27.translation: Thus addressed by the sage Sharabhanga, Rama, tiger among men and learned in all scriptures, replied:
ramayana-3-4-27.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-28.translation: 'Great sage, I will win all those worlds myself. But I would like a dwelling place pointed out to me here in the forest.'
ramayana-3-4-28.meaning: Rama declined another's merit and asked only for a place to live.
ramayana-3-4-28.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world. Rama prefers to earn rather than receive spiritual reward.

ramayana-3-4-29.translation: Thus addressed by Rama, whose strength equalled Indra's, the wise Sharabhanga spoke again:
ramayana-3-4-29.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-30.translation: 'Go to the ascetic Sutikshna, in a pure place in a lovely part of the forest; he will arrange a dwelling for you.
ramayana-3-4-30.meaning: He sent Rama to another sage.
ramayana-3-4-30.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-31.translation: This is the path, tiger among men. Watch me for a moment, dear one, while I leave my limbs as a snake sheds its old skin.'
ramayana-3-4-31.meaning: The sage prepared to give up his body.
ramayana-3-4-31.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-32.translation: Then the mighty Sharabhanga, who knew the mantras, kindled the fire, made an offering of ghee and entered the fire.
ramayana-3-4-32.meaning: He entered the fire as a final offering.
ramayana-3-4-32.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-33.translation: The fire burned the great soul's body hair, his hair, his old skin, bones, flesh and blood.
ramayana-3-4-33.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-34.translation: And Sharabhanga became a youth bright as fire, and rising from the pyre he shone.
ramayana-3-4-34.meaning: He rose renewed, shining and young.
ramayana-3-4-34.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-35.translation: Passing beyond the worlds of those who keep sacred fires, of great sages and of the gods, he ascended to Brahma's world.
ramayana-3-4-35.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-4-36.translation: That best of brahmins, of holy deeds, saw the Grandfather Brahma with his attendants in that world; and Brahma, seeing him, rejoiced and said, 'Welcome!'
ramayana-3-4-36.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 4: Indra leaves as Rama arrives; the sage Sharabhanga, who had waited to see Rama, sends him to Sutikshna and then enters the fire and rises to Brahma's world.

ramayana-3-5-1.translation: When Sharabhanga had gone to heaven, groups of sages gathered and came to Rama, who was blazing with energy.
ramayana-3-5-1.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-2.translation: There were Vaikhanasas, Valakhilyas, Samprakshalas, Marichipas, many Ashmakuttas and ascetics who lived on leaves,
ramayana-3-5-2.meaning: The forest held many kinds of ascetic.
ramayana-3-5-2.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them. The list names different ascetic disciplines.

ramayana-3-5-3.translation: others who used their teeth as mortars, others who stood immersed in water, sages who lived on water and others who lived on air,
ramayana-3-5-3.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-4.translation: those who lived in the open sky, those who slept on bare ground, those who stood upright, the self-controlled, and those who wore wet clothes,
ramayana-3-5-4.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-5.translation: those devoted to chanting and constant austerity, and those who practised the five fires; all endowed with spiritual splendour and firm in yoga, these ascetics came to Rama at Sharabhanga's hermitage.
ramayana-3-5-5.meaning: All came together to see Rama.
ramayana-3-5-5.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-6.translation: Approaching Rama, best of those who uphold dharma, the groups of sages who knew dharma spoke with composure:
ramayana-3-5-6.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-7.translation: 'You are the great warrior of the Ikshvaku line and of the earth, its chief and protector, as Indra is of the gods.
ramayana-3-5-7.meaning: They honoured Rama as their protector.
ramayana-3-5-7.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-8.translation: You are famed in the three worlds for glory and valour; in you are devotion to your father, truth and abundant dharma.
ramayana-3-5-8.meaning: Rama is known for truth and loyalty.
ramayana-3-5-8.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-9.translation: Having come to you, great soul who knows and loves dharma, we will speak as petitioners, lord; please forgive us.
ramayana-3-5-9.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-10.translation: Great is the wrong of a king who takes a sixth of the produce as tax and does not protect his people like his own sons.
ramayana-3-5-10.meaning: A ruler who taxes but does not protect does great wrong.
ramayana-3-5-10.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-11.translation: But one who cares for all who live in his realm as for his own life, or for his beloved sons, always attentive and protecting,
ramayana-3-5-11.meaning: A good ruler cares for his people as for his own children.
ramayana-3-5-11.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-12.translation: such a king wins lasting fame for many years, Rama, reaches the realm of Brahma and is honoured there.
ramayana-3-5-12.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-13.translation: Of the high dharma that a sage living on roots and fruits performs, a fourth part goes to the king who protects his people rightly.
ramayana-3-5-13.meaning: The protector shares in the good of those he protects.
ramayana-3-5-13.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-14.translation: This great company of forest hermits, mostly brahmins, has you as protector, yet is being killed by demons as if it had none.
ramayana-3-5-14.meaning: The sages are suffering though Rama is their king.
ramayana-3-5-14.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-15.translation: Come and see the bodies of many sages of purified soul, killed in many ways by terrible demons in the forest.
ramayana-3-5-15.meaning: They showed him the evidence of the killings.
ramayana-3-5-15.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-16.translation: Great slaughter is being done to those who live by the Pampa river, along the Mandakini, and on Chitrakuta.
ramayana-3-5-16.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-17.translation: We cannot bear the terrible harm being done to ascetics in the forest by demons of dreadful deeds.
ramayana-3-5-17.meaning: They can no longer endure it.
ramayana-3-5-17.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-18.translation: So we have come to you, our refuge, seeking shelter. Protect us, Rama, who are being killed by night-roamers.'
ramayana-3-5-18.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-19.translation: Hearing this from the ascetics, the righteous Rama said to them all: 'You should not speak to me like this; I am to be commanded by ascetics.
ramayana-3-5-19.meaning: Rama humbly placed himself at their service.
ramayana-3-5-19.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-20.translation: I have come by chance to fulfil your purpose; this stay of mine in the forest will bear great fruit. I wish to kill in battle the demons who are enemies of ascetics.'
ramayana-3-5-20.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-5-21.translation: Having given his promise to the ascetics, the hero, steadfast in dharma, went with Lakshmana and the ascetics to Sutikshna.
ramayana-3-5-21.meaning: Rama set out with his promise made.
ramayana-3-5-21.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 5: a great gathering of forest ascetics tells Rama how demons are killing them, and Rama promises to protect them.

ramayana-3-6-1.translation: Rama, scorcher of foes, with his brother and Sita, went to Sutikshna's hermitage with those brahmins.
ramayana-3-6-1.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-2.translation: After travelling a long way and crossing rivers full of water, he saw a vast mountain rising like a great cloud.
ramayana-3-6-2.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-3.translation: Then the two best of the Ikshvakus, with Sita, entered a forest always full of many kinds of trees.
ramayana-3-6-3.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-4.translation: Entering the deep forest full of flowering and fruiting trees, he saw a secluded hermitage hung with strings of bark garments.
ramayana-3-6-4.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-5.translation: There Rama formally addressed the ascetic Sutikshna, seated, bearing matted hair caked with dirt, grown great in austerity.
ramayana-3-6-5.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-6.translation: 'I am Rama, holy one; I have come to see you. Speak to me, knower of dharma, great seer of true valour.'
ramayana-3-6-6.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-7.translation: Looking at the hero Rama, best of upholders of dharma, he embraced him with both arms and said:
ramayana-3-6-7.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-8.translation: 'Welcome, hero Rama, best of upholders of dharma; now that you have come, this hermitage has found its protector.
ramayana-3-6-8.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-9.translation: Waiting for you, glorious one, I did not leave my body on earth to rise to the world of the gods.
ramayana-3-6-9.meaning: He too had waited to see Rama.
ramayana-3-6-9.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-10.translation: I heard you had lost your kingdom and gone to Chitrakuta. Indra, king of the gods, came here and said I had won all worlds by my holy deeds.
ramayana-3-6-10.meaning: He told Rama of Indra's visit.
ramayana-3-6-10.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-11.translation: By my grace, enjoy with your wife and Lakshmana those worlds frequented by divine seers that I have won by austerity.'
ramayana-3-6-11.meaning: He offered his merit to Rama.
ramayana-3-6-11.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-12.translation: Self-possessed Rama answered that fierce, radiant, truthful sage, as Indra answers Brahma:
ramayana-3-6-12.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-13.translation: 'Great sage, I will win the worlds myself. But I would like a dwelling place pointed out to me here in the forest.
ramayana-3-6-13.meaning: Again Rama asked only for a place to stay.
ramayana-3-6-13.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-14.translation: You are skilled in everything and devoted to the good of all beings, as the great Sharabhanga Gautama told me.'
ramayana-3-6-14.meaning: Rama explained who had sent him.
ramayana-3-6-14.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-15.translation: Thus addressed by Rama, the world-famous great seer, flooded with joy, spoke sweet words:
ramayana-3-6-15.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-16.translation: 'This very hermitage is good, Rama; enjoy yourself here. It is frequented by groups of sages and always has roots and fruits.
ramayana-3-6-16.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-17.translation: Herds of deer come to this hermitage, glorious one, roam about fearless and go away again, tempting us.
ramayana-3-6-17.meaning: Even the animals live here without fear.
ramayana-3-6-17.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-18.translation: Hearing these words of the great seer, Rama, Lakshmana's elder brother, drew his bow with its arrow and said firmly:
ramayana-3-6-18.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-19.translation: 'If I were to kill those herds of deer that come here with my sharp-edged arrow bright as lightning,
ramayana-3-6-19.meaning: Rama noted that hunters like him would disturb the peace.
ramayana-3-6-19.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-20.translation: you would be distressed; what could be worse than that? So I do not think I should stay long in this hermitage.'
ramayana-3-6-20.meaning: Rama would not stay where he might cause harm.
ramayana-3-6-20.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage. Rama respects the hermitage's non-violence.

ramayana-3-6-21.translation: Having said this to the giver of boons, Rama went to his evening prayers; after the western twilight rite he prepared to stay there.
ramayana-3-6-21.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-6-22.translation: Then, seeing night had come after the twilight rites, the great-souled Sutikshna himself gave the two best of men fine ascetics' food, with great honour.
ramayana-3-6-22.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 6: Rama reaches the sage Sutikshna, who welcomes him and offers him his hermitage.

ramayana-3-7-1.translation: Rama and Lakshmana, honoured by Sutikshna, spent the night there and woke at dawn.
ramayana-3-7-1.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-2.translation: Rising at the proper time, Rama with Sita bathed in cool water fragrant with lotuses.
ramayana-3-7-2.meaning: They began the day with purification.
ramayana-3-7-2.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-3.translation: Then Sita, Rama and Lakshmana duly worshipped the fire and the gods at dawn in the forest, the refuge of ascetics,
ramayana-3-7-3.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-4.translation: and seeing the rising sun, freed from impurity, they approached Sutikshna and spoke gently:
ramayana-3-7-4.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-5.translation: 'We have lived happily, holy one, honoured by you who are worthy of honour. We take our leave and will go; the sages are urging us on.
ramayana-3-7-5.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-6.translation: We are eager to see the whole circle of hermitages of the virtuous sages who live in the Dandaka forest.
ramayana-3-7-6.meaning: They wished to visit all the sages.
ramayana-3-7-6.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-7.translation: We wish your leave to go with these best of sages, devoted to dharma, restrained by austerity, like fires without smoke.
ramayana-3-7-7.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-8.translation: before the sun grows too fierce with unbearable heat, like a low-born man who has gained wealth by wrong means,
ramayana-3-7-8.meaning: They wanted to set off before the heat.
ramayana-3-7-8.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest. The simile compares harsh sun to arrogance from ill-gotten wealth.

ramayana-3-7-9.translation: we wish to go.' Saying this, Rama with Lakshmana and Sita bowed at the sage's feet.
ramayana-3-7-9.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-10.translation: The best of sages raised the two who were touching his feet, embraced them tightly and lovingly, and said:
ramayana-3-7-10.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-11.translation: 'Go safely on your way, Rama, with Lakshmana and this Sita who follows you like a shadow.
ramayana-3-7-11.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-12.translation: See the lovely hermitages of the ascetics of the Dandaka forest, hero, whose souls are purified by austerity.
ramayana-3-7-12.meaning: He encouraged them to see the hermitages.
ramayana-3-7-12.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-13.translation: forests rich in fruits and roots and full of flowers, with calm herds of deer and peaceful flocks of birds,
ramayana-3-7-13.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-14.translation: lakes and ponds with clear water, full of blooming lotuses and scattered with karandava ducks,
ramayana-3-7-14.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-15.translation: You will see mountain springs lovely to look at, and charming forests filled with the cries of peacocks.
ramayana-3-7-15.meaning: The forest was full of delights.
ramayana-3-7-15.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-16.translation: Go, dear child; and you too, Lakshmana. Having seen them, come back to my hermitage again.'
ramayana-3-7-16.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-17.translation: Saying 'So be it', Rama with Lakshmana walked around the sage respectfully and prepared to set out.
ramayana-3-7-17.meaning: They circled the sage in respect.
ramayana-3-7-17.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-18.translation: Then the large-eyed Sita handed the two brothers their fine quivers, their bows and their bright swords.
ramayana-3-7-18.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-7-19.translation: Binding on their fine quivers and taking up their twanging bows, Rama and Lakshmana left the hermitage to go.
ramayana-3-7-19.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 7: after a night at Sutikshna's hermitage, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana take leave to visit the other hermitages of the Dandaka forest.

ramayana-3-8-1.translation: As Rama set out with Sutikshna's leave, Sita spoke to her husband in an affectionate voice:
ramayana-3-8-1.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-2.translation: 'This great dharma is reached by very subtle means; and here one can keep it only by turning away from the vices born of desire.
ramayana-3-8-2.meaning: Dharma is subtle and needs self-restraint.
ramayana-3-8-2.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-3.translation: There are three vices born of desire: lying is the first, and two are heavier still, going to another's wife, and cruelty without enmity.
ramayana-3-8-3.meaning: Sita names three faults: lying, adultery and violence without cause.
ramayana-3-8-3.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-4.translation: Falsehood you have never spoken and never will, Rama; how then could you desire other men's wives, which destroys dharma?
ramayana-3-8-4.meaning: Sita knows Rama is free of the first two faults.
ramayana-3-8-4.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-5.translation: All this can be borne by those who master their senses, mighty-armed one; and I know your senses are under your control, handsome one.
ramayana-3-8-5.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-6.translation: The third, this cruelty of taking others' lives without enmity, done through delusion, is now before you.
ramayana-3-8-6.meaning: Sita worries Rama may harm those who have not harmed him.
ramayana-3-8-6.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity. This is Sita's ethical caution about violence, one of the epic's notable debates.

ramayana-3-8-7.translation: You have promised, hero, to kill demons in battle to protect the sages of the Dandaka forest.
ramayana-3-8-7.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-8.translation: For this purpose you have set out with your brother, carrying bow and arrows, for the forest known as Dandaka.
ramayana-3-8-8.meaning: He goes armed for that purpose.
ramayana-3-8-8.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-9.translation: Seeing you set out, my mind is troubled with worry, thinking about your conduct and what will truly be for your highest good.
ramayana-3-8-9.meaning: Sita speaks out of love and concern.
ramayana-3-8-9.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-10.translation: I do not like this going to the Dandaka forest, hero. I will tell you the reason; listen as I speak.
ramayana-3-8-10.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-11.translation: You have gone into the forest with your brother, bow and arrows in hand; seeing all the forest creatures, might you not spend your arrows on them?
ramayana-3-8-11.meaning: She fears weapons tempt one to use them.
ramayana-3-8-11.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-12.translation: Here a kshatriya's bow is like fuel for fire: when kept close, it greatly increases one's fierce energy.
ramayana-3-8-12.meaning: Having weapons at hand can stir aggression.
ramayana-3-8-12.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-13.translation: Long ago, mighty-armed one, there was a truthful and pure ascetic in a holy forest where deer and birds were happy.
ramayana-3-8-13.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-14.translation: To obstruct his austerity, Indra, husband of Shachi, came to the hermitage disguised as a soldier, sword in hand.
ramayana-3-8-14.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-15.translation: He left that fine sword in the hermitage, given as a deposit in trust to the sage who was engaged in holy austerity.
ramayana-3-8-15.meaning: The ascetic was asked to keep the sword safe.
ramayana-3-8-15.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-16.translation: Having received that weapon and intent on guarding the deposit, he carried it around the forest, keeping faith.
ramayana-3-8-16.meaning: He kept the sword with him always.
ramayana-3-8-16.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-17.translation: Wherever he went to gather roots and fruits, he never went without that sword, intent on guarding the trust.
ramayana-3-8-17.meaning: The sword never left his side.
ramayana-3-8-17.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-18.translation: Always carrying the weapon, the ascetic gradually turned his mind to cruelty, giving up his resolve in austerity.
ramayana-3-8-18.meaning: Constant contact with a weapon changed his nature.
ramayana-3-8-18.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-19.translation: Then, delighting in cruelty, careless and dragged down by wrongdoing, the sage went to hell through his association with the weapon.
ramayana-3-8-19.meaning: He fell through what he kept close.
ramayana-3-8-19.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity. The story teaches that what we keep near us shapes who we become.

ramayana-3-8-20.translation: I remind you out of love and great respect, not to teach you; never make up your mind, bow in hand,
ramayana-3-8-20.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-21.translation: to kill demons living in Dandaka without enmity. I do not want you to kill beings who have done no wrong, hero.
ramayana-3-8-21.meaning: Do not harm those who have not harmed you.
ramayana-3-8-21.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-22.translation: For heroic kshatriyas living with restraint in the forest, this is all the bow is for: protecting the suffering.
ramayana-3-8-22.meaning: A weapon's only right use is to protect.
ramayana-3-8-22.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-23.translation: Where is the weapon and where the forest, where the warrior's way and where austerity? These do not go together; let us honour the dharma of the place we are in.
ramayana-3-8-23.meaning: Live by the spirit of where you are.
ramayana-3-8-23.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-24.translation: Handling weapons makes the mind of a noble person turbid. When you return to Ayodhya, then you can follow the warrior's duty.
ramayana-3-8-24.meaning: Keep the warrior's role for its proper place.
ramayana-3-8-24.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-25.translation: My mother-in-law and father-in-law would have unending joy if, having set aside the kingdom, you lived here devoted as a sage.
ramayana-3-8-25.meaning: Living as a sage in exile would please the family.
ramayana-3-8-25.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-26.translation: From dharma comes wealth, from dharma comes happiness; by dharma one gains everything; dharma is the essence of this world.
ramayana-3-8-26.meaning: Rightness is the root of every good.
ramayana-3-8-26.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity. A widely quoted line on dharma.

ramayana-3-8-27.translation: The wise reach dharma by carefully disciplining themselves with various restraints; happiness is not gained through comfort.
ramayana-3-8-27.meaning: Real happiness comes through discipline, not ease.
ramayana-3-8-27.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-28.translation: Gentle one, practise dharma in the ascetics' forest always with a pure mind; for you truly know everything, even the three worlds.
ramayana-3-8-28.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity.

ramayana-3-8-29.translation: I have said this out of a woman's restlessness; who could teach you dharma? Think it over with your brother and do quickly what seems right.
ramayana-3-8-29.meaning: Sita humbly leaves the decision to Rama.
ramayana-3-8-29.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 8: Sita gently questions whether Rama should take up arms against beings who have not harmed him, warning about violence without enmity. Sita's self-deprecating phrase reflects the conventions of her time; her argument itself is serious and Rama treats it with respect.

ramayana-3-9-1.translation: Hearing these words spoken by Sita, devoted to her husband, Rama, steadfast in dharma, answered her:
ramayana-3-9-1.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-2.translation: 'Queen, you have spoken good, affectionate words worthy of you and of your family, knower of dharma, daughter of Janaka.
ramayana-3-9-2.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-3.translation: But what shall I say, queen? You yourself said it: kshatriyas carry the bow so that no cry of distress is heard.
ramayana-3-9-3.meaning: Rama uses Sita's own point: the bow protects the suffering.
ramayana-3-9-3.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-4.translation: And those sages in the Dandaka, firm in their vows, are in distress; they came to me themselves, Sita, the refuges seeking refuge.
ramayana-3-9-4.meaning: The sages are the suffering ones.
ramayana-3-9-4.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-5.translation: Living in the forest devoted to dharma, eating roots and fruits, they find no happiness, afraid of cruel demons.
ramayana-3-9-5.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-6.translation: Time and again, those devoted to many disciplines in the forest are eaten by dreadful demons who live on human flesh.
ramayana-3-9-6.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-7.translation: Being devoured, those best of brahmins living in the Dandaka said to me, 'Help us.'
ramayana-3-9-7.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-8.translation: Hearing these words from their mouths, I served at their feet and said this:
ramayana-3-9-8.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-9.translation: 'Be gracious to me; I feel boundless shame that such brahmins, whom I should approach, have approached me. What shall I do?' I said before the brahmins.
ramayana-3-9-9.meaning: Rama felt ashamed that the sages had to come to him.
ramayana-3-9-9.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-10.translation: Gathering together, they all said: 'We are sorely oppressed by many shape-shifting demons in the Dandaka forest, Rama; you must save us.
ramayana-3-9-10.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-11.translation: When the time for offerings comes, and on holy days, sinless one, the invincible flesh-eating demons attack us.
ramayana-3-9-11.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-12.translation: For us ascetics attacked by demons and seeking a way out, you are our highest refuge.
ramayana-3-9-12.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-13.translation: We could indeed kill the night-roamers by the power of our austerity, but we do not wish to spend the austerity we have gathered over long years.
ramayana-3-9-13.meaning: The sages will not use their spiritual power for harm.
ramayana-3-9-13.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-14.translation: Austerity is always full of obstacles and hard to practise, Rama; so we do not utter curses, even while being eaten by demons.
ramayana-3-9-14.meaning: They keep their peace even when suffering.
ramayana-3-9-14.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-15.translation: So protect us, with your brother, who are tormented by the demons of Dandaka; in the forest you are our protector.'
ramayana-3-9-15.meaning: They asked Rama to protect them.
ramayana-3-9-15.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-16.translation: Hearing these words, daughter of Janaka, I promised the sages of Dandaka full protection.
ramayana-3-9-16.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-17.translation: Having promised, I cannot, while I live, go back on my word to the sages; truth is always dear to me.
ramayana-3-9-17.meaning: A promise once given must be kept.
ramayana-3-9-17.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-18.translation: I would give up my life, or even you, Sita, and Lakshmana, but I would not break a promise once made, especially one made to brahmins.
ramayana-3-9-18.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise. This hyperbole expresses how sacred Rama holds a promise.

ramayana-3-9-19.translation: So I must protect the sages; even unasked I would do it, Sita, how much more having promised.
ramayana-3-9-19.meaning: Duty and promise both call him.
ramayana-3-9-19.explanation: Aranya Kanda, chapter 9: Rama answers Sita, explaining that he has given his word to protect the sages and will never break a promise.

ramayana-3-9-20.translation: You said this out of love and friendship for me; I am pleased, Sita, for no one advises someone they do not care for. It is fitting and worthy of your family, lovely one.'
ramayana-3-9-20.meaning: Rama honours Sita's concern as an act of love.
